reading.ours: two units of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — an instrument check, and it is printed first because nothing below it means anything until it passes. The true ratio is a little UNDER 2: both sides pay the driving loop once, so the exact expectation is (2u + L) / (u + L) with L the loop and u one unit, which at sixteen dependent steps per unit puts it around 1.9. A reading below 1.5 means this process could not resolve a deliberate doubling, and the runner voids the report rather than printing prices under it.

reading.ours: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: the same body again, over its own copy of the same state
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — the noise floor. The two sides are identical code over identical, separately-allocated state, so the true ratio is 1.00 exactly and every departure from it printed here was produced by this machine at this moment. The rule that follows is the one the whole table is read under: NO RATIO CLOSER TO 1.00 THAN THIS GAP IS A READING. It also bounds the per-row noise figure, which is the same idea measured again inside every pair — each pair times its floor twice, once before our side and once after, and prints how far the two disagreed.

reading.floor: the same Set, at fan-in 3 — two arrivals in three are repeats

reading.floor: rows.get(key)
reading.caveat: ONE INDIRECTION MORE ON OUR SIDE: the row sits on the slot, so a read by key is a hash and a field load where the two-map store answers with the hash alone. reading.floor: rows.set(key, row); then identities.get(key) because that map is no longer empty
reading.caveat: WHERE THE BILL FOR TWO MAPS ARRIVES. reading.caveat: THE MEMO WITH NOTHING TO AMORTISE OVER: a filter and a sum over the list, read once per write, so ours derives on every read exactly as the floor does and pays the node on top. reading.ours: a member leaves a bucket of 100 and joins another, membership in a Set (OIMBucketSlotsServiceSetDriven)
reading.floor: the same move, membership in a list kept in the caller's order (OIMBucketSlotsServiceArrayDriven)
reading.caveat: A BUCKET OF 100, and the size is in the id because the answer is a function of it on BOTH halves. THE COUNT THIS PREDICTS, per member moved, through `bucketCollection.writeContent`: on the ordered half, `reconcile` compares the held list against the one handed in up to the swapped band, finds them unequal, drains all 100 members and pushes all 100 back, and the collection holds 100 arrivals and unholds 100 departures. On the unordered half: `reconcile` builds one Set of the 100 slots handed in, probes it once per held member, deletes the one departure and adds the one arrival, and one hold is taken and one given back. The ordered half's sequence comparison stops at the swapped band, which is why the sweep over 16 positions (0, 6, 12, … 90) exists: it averages that comparison length. ONE FLUSH IS SPREAD OVER 64 OPERATIONS, since a frame swaps one band in every lane at once; `flush.empty-vs-noop` prices a flush directly, for a reader who wants it out of the figure. WHAT AN OPERATION IS: one member moves from one bucket to another, through the only door the engine offers for it — two array stores that exchange the member between the two lists this file holds, `bucketCollection.writeContent` of each of those lists, a flush, and a read of every bucket in the frame through `getBucketMemberSlots`. Both halves run the identical body; the only difference in the process is which bucket service object the collection was constructed with. READINGS RECORDED BEFORE 2026-08-23 priced a re-file reached through a derived membership source and are not this operation. EVERY OPERATION REALLY MOVES A MEMBER, which is the failure this suite has already published a wrong number for: `writeContent` RETURNS without a wake when `reconcile` finds nothing arrived and nothing departed, and both halves would then time a frame in which no container was touched. Here the two lists handed in differ from what the buckets hold by exactly one member each, and `assertBandsAreWhereTheyAreExpected` checks each bucket holds exactly the members this file holds for it before the clock starts. The two rows of a swap are the two members of one band, one in each page of the lane, and the swap exchanges them — which is why this needs no `reset` at all: sizes, positions and the sweep are exactly what they were when the pass started, so an empty reset here is a steady state rather than a forgotten one. DIRECTION, three ways. (1) The two array stores, the mark, the flush and the read call are identical in SHAPE on both halves and inside both numbers, which pulls the RATIO toward 1.00, so the two printed nanosecond figures are the numbers to read. (2) ONLY THE SET HALF DIFFS: `OIMBucketSlotsServiceSetDriven.reconcile` takes the set difference (one Set of the list handed in, one probe per held member) and moves one hold each way, while the ordered half's `reconcile` compares the two sequences up to the first mismatch, then drains the whole list and re-adds every member, so every member it holds is unheld and held again. READINGS RECORDED BEFORE 2026-10-17 timed a set half that drained and refilled the whole set and an ordered half that kept a rank sorter and took a multiset difference, and are not this operation. (3) Both containers are walked every frame and stay in cache, which flatters both. A PASS IS WHOLE FRAMES, because half a swap would leave both members of a band in one page and every position after it would be a lie; so a pass may overshoot the operation count the prober asked for by fewer operations than there are pages, out of the tens of thousands it asks for.

THE COUNT THIS PREDICTS, per member moved, through `bucketCollection.writeContent`: on the ordered half, `reconcile` compares the held list against the one handed in up to the swapped band, finds them unequal, drains all 50000 members and pushes all 50000 back, and the collection holds 50000 arrivals and unholds 50000 departures. On the unordered half: `reconcile` builds one Set of the 50000 slots handed in, probes it once per held member, deletes the one departure and adds the one arrival, and one hold is taken and one given back. The ordered half's sequence comparison stops at the swapped band, which is why the sweep over 16 positions (0, 3125, 6250, … 46875) exists: it averages that comparison length. ONE FLUSH IS SPREAD OVER 2 OPERATIONS, since a frame swaps one band in every lane at once; `flush.empty-vs-noop` prices a flush directly, for a reader who wants it out of the figure. WHAT AN OPERATION IS: one member moves from one bucket to another, through the only door the engine offers for it — two array stores that exchange the member between the two lists this file holds, `bucketCollection.writeContent` of each of those lists, a flush, and a read of every bucket in the frame through `getBucketMemberSlots`. Both halves run the identical body; the only difference in the process is which bucket service object the collection was constructed with. READINGS RECORDED BEFORE 2026-08-23 priced a re-file reached through a derived membership source and are not this operation. EVERY OPERATION REALLY MOVES A MEMBER, which is the failure this suite has already published a wrong number for: `writeContent` RETURNS without a wake when `reconcile` finds nothing arrived and nothing departed, and both halves would then time a frame in which no container was touched. Here the two lists handed in differ from what the buckets hold by exactly one member each, and `assertBandsAreWhereTheyAreExpected` checks each bucket holds exactly the members this file holds for it before the clock starts. The two rows of a swap are the two members of one band, one in each page of the lane, and the swap exchanges them — which is why this needs no `reset` at all: sizes, positions and the sweep are exactly what they were when the pass started, so an empty reset here is a steady state rather than a forgotten one. DIRECTION, three ways. (1) The two array stores, the mark, the flush and the read call are identical in SHAPE on both halves and inside both numbers, which pulls the RATIO toward 1.00, so the two printed nanosecond figures are the numbers to read. (2) ONLY THE SET HALF DIFFS: `OIMBucketSlotsServiceSetDriven.reconcile` takes the set difference (one Set of the list handed in, one probe per held member) and moves one hold each way, while the ordered half's `reconcile` compares the two sequences up to the first mismatch, then drains the whole list and re-adds every member, so every member it holds is unheld and held again. READINGS RECORDED BEFORE 2026-10-17 timed a set half that drained and refilled the whole set and an ordered half that kept a rank sorter and took a multiset difference, and are not this operation. (3) Both containers are walked every frame and stay in cache, which flatters both. A PASS IS WHOLE FRAMES, because half a swap would leave both members of a band in one page and every position after it would be a lie; so a pass may overshoot the operation count the prober asked for by fewer operations than there are pages, out of the tens of thousands it asks for.

reading.ours: for (const slot of bucketCollection.getBucketMemberSlots(bucket)) slot.entity — a Set of 10000, per member
reading.floor: the same walk of the same members, kept as a list, per member
reading.caveat: THE SENTENCE UNDER TEST is the one printed above the published removal table: "Both iterate at around [NO RUN BEHIND THIS FIGURE] 2 ns per element, and the difference between them is a fraction of that." It is the half of the bucket service argument that says the choice is NOT an iteration question, and it had no measurement behind it either. THE BODY IS THE SAME ON BOTH HALVES, character for character: one `getBucketMemberSlots`, one for-of, one field load and one store into the sink per member. The only difference in the process is what `getBucketMemberSlots` hands back — a `Set` on ours, the service's own array on the floor — so this row is a property of two JavaScript containers reached through one library, which is exactly what the sentence claims to be about. NOTHING IS WRITTEN, NO MEMBERSHIP IS SET AND NO FRAME IS CLOSED, and neither service orders anything on a read: the list hands back the array `priceGroupIndex` filled, in the order it was written. What a pass pays outside the walk is one service call and one iterator, spread over 10000 members. DIRECTION, three ways: (1) ours is measured on a set that was FILLED and never deleted from, so its entry table has no tombstones to walk — a bucket that has churned iterates worse, and this row therefore flatters the unordered half; (2) `slot.entity` is loaded per member on both halves, because a reader that visits members without looking at them is not a reader, and it is the same monomorphic field load on each side; (3) a pass is a whole walk of the bucket, so the operation count may overshoot what the prober asked for by fewer than 10000 members out of the millions a [NO RUN BEHIND THIS FIGURE] 25 ms pass visits.

reading.ours: write 300 roots, then read 200 computeds that walk their 3 sources — chain depth 1
reading.floor: the same writes, each marking its dependents dirty; each read is one boolean — depth 1
reading.caveat: THE ROW THE RECOVERED RUN ACTUALLY COVERED, REBUILT SO THE OTHER TWO HAVE SOMETHING TO BE READ AGAINST. Its figure at this geometry was 0.72x in our favour [NO RUN BEHIND THIS FIGURE], and the whole reason the other two rows exist is that this one was the ONLY depth measured. At depth 1 push is at its strongest: a consumer is one boolean away from knowing it owes a derivation, and the sources under it are roots, which are current by definition — so the arm has nothing to descend and nothing to bring up to date. If the recovered figure is going to reproduce anywhere it is here, and a reading far from it on this row means the two runs are not measuring the same thing and the other two rows should not be quoted either [FIGURE STATED IN ADVANCE]. RESIDUALS. AGAINST US, AND THEY ARE THE MAJORITY: our arm is the SHIPPED `OIMComputedCollection`, one per level, each node a held computed slot read through `getValueForSlot`, so every read pays `assertNotReleased` and a call into `oimRefreshComputedSlot`; every refresh that misses the clock pays `oimRefreshSourceComputeds`, a call into `oimHasSourceChangedSinceLastRun`, a call into `oimIsRevisionAfter` per source, a call into the comparator, `isDeriving` written twice and THREE pairs of stamps written per derivation (`ranAt*`, `checkedAt*` and `changedAt*`) — the rejected arm carries one boolean and writes it once. Above level one the derive reads each source computed through its owner AGAIN, after `oimRefreshSourceComputeds` already brought it current, so each such source costs one more `getValueForSlot` that returns on its `checkedAt` pair, and the derive finds its source list by the slot's key. Our nodes are also filed as slots in a `Map` per level, with `effects`, `holdCount`, `owner` and `key` on every one of them, and the rejected node has none of that. AGAINST THE REJECTED ARM: nothing, except that it walks a recursive `markDependents` where a real engine might flatten it. WHAT NEITHER ARM PAYS: the frame. No effect is subscribed and `channel.flush()` is never called, so the leaf list, the drain and the after-frame phases are on neither side — a frame is priced by `flush.empty-vs-noop` and adding it to both halves of a ratio only pulls it toward 1. WHAT IS NOT EXERCISED, and it is the design difference that no timing here can show: push marks the WHOLE transitive cone at the write, while pull stops at the first computed whose value held. Every root moves every frame here and every sum therefore changes, so the comparator never cuts anything on either arm and push is never charged for a mark it did not owe. A graph where a change is absorbed part-way up is the arrangement in which push is at its worst, and it is not measured. NOR IS THE CONSUMER AXIS: the recovered table reported the two converging where ten consumers share one computed, and every node here is read by exactly one consumer.

reading.ours: mint one slot of each of the three shipped shapes
reading.floor: mint three slots of the one unified shape
reading.caveat: THE HALF OF THE UNIFIED-SHAPE ARGUMENT THAT PAYS FOR IT. One operation mints three literals; the unified one carries every field of every kind, so it is larger than every shipped kind, and a first load pays that once per entity. Both arms allocate inside the clock and the young-generation collections that follow are charged to whichever arm allocated more, which is the honest direction. Divide this pair's difference by the write pair's difference to get the writes per slot at which the unified shape breaks even.

reading.ours: effectService.createEffect([slot], [], body) then effectService.disposeEffect(effect) — per subscriber
reading.floor: emitter.subscribeOnKey(key, body) then the returned unsubscribe — 3.12.1
reading.caveat: ONE OPERATION IS ONE SUBSCRIBER MOUNTED AND RELEASED, in batches of the churn family's largest count on one identity. Ours allocates a `TOIMEffect` per mount, appends it to the slot's `effects` array, holds the slot, and on dispose swap-removes it and unholds; 3.12.1 adds the handler to the carrier's `Set` and the carrier to the emitter's subscribed set, and its unsubscribe closure deletes both. Every body is a distinct closure, because the 3.12.1 `Set` collapses one function subscribed many times into one handler. Neither arm writes or flushes.

reading.ours: channel.write(slot); channel.flush() — every effect on the slot runs
reading.floor: emitter.markUpdatedKey(key); queue.flush() — every handler on the carrier runs — 3.12.1
reading.caveat: ONE OPERATION IS ONE SUBSCRIBER WOKEN; a frame wakes the whole standing set, mounted before the clock. Ours stamps the slot, enlists each effect through its pending flag, and at the flush asks each effect whether its source moved since it last ran — a stamp compare — before calling its body. 3.12.1 marks the carrier dirty once, and its flush iterates the carrier's handler `Set` and calls each. Both arms were checked to wake every subscriber exactly once per write before the clock started. Neither arm goes through a collection write: this is the subscription cost alone, not the write stack in front of it.
